game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
The premise is simple:
It's a game where you play a investigator who works for the government, sifting through data in all of its forms in order to fight for the safety of the public in the fictional world that it's set in.

There have been many 'hacking' games that have come out over the years, but Orwell takes the idea and puts you in the position of 'good' rather than 'bad', which creates the core ideology of the game -- If what you're doing is so good, then why do you feel so bad doing it?

The game proceeds along a UI of sorts, one that allows you to sift through websites, personal pages and even listen on some incredibly well-simulated 'real time chats', along with interruptions and intentional spelling errors that betray the typer's emotions and mental states. It's one of the best simulations of texting I've seen before in a game, and it DOES stand out. The articles and websites, while simple and clean, are detailed and packed full of worldbuilding -- the developers go out of their way to fill the world with detail that was never necessary to get from point A to B, but still fill everything with life and activity, and the world ends up feeling a little bit less compartmentalized than other games which force you into a limited POV.

However, this all leads back to the internal condundrum I have with this game:
You work with a handler who analyses the information you send him, and it's his job to make sense of it all. All you do is forward him the pertinent information, enough for him to make decisions and calls on how to handle situations. And you must choose what it is you want to send.

It's your choice to pick A over B. And it's not outright lies, because you're the good guy, remember? But whatever you send can tinge a thought, affect outcomes and colour perceptions in slight, yet pertinent, ways. Your own analysis plays a big part in how you want to portray someone else, and ultimately, the only one who has to live with the decisions you make is yourself.

Orwell is a great game about people, but more than that, it's a platform to help you examine yourself as a person. Since you're doing this for the percieved good, what decisions will you make and how far will you go to get what you want? And is there ever a time when personal freedom can be infringed upon for the greater result? Well... that might be another question for another time.

It's a good game tho, eh?

(( P.S.: Like any other 'visual novel' style game, and including the horrendous works of Mr. David Cage, I am fully aware that some of these 'choices' may be nothing more than illusionary. However, the game does it well enough in its context that reflecting upon the choices you make actually makes more than just a surface-level difference since you're playing not a character, but yourself. And considering the game's name and influences, I believe this to be the point. ))

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is pretty fascinating, and I am looking forward to the next episodes (this is being released in episodes, bit by bit). Basically, you are being "Big Brother", hacking into personal files, browsing social media sites in order to solve and prevent crimes. 

Surely, there is a pretty obvious message here, which might be a bit too moralistic for some, but then again, I find it fascinating how you can actually upload unclear information (which is in conflict with another bit of information) and thereby push the investigation into the wrong direction.

Example: One guy mentions "torture", but didn't mean actual physical torture, but more like "it was torture to wait", more like in a fun way. However, if you pull that term and upload it, you will convince your superiors that the person is actually into torturing other people, thereby painting a totally wrong picture, distorting the facts. 
Which is what actually happens a lot, not only on the web, irl. 

The game has a certain indie, Papers Please type vibe... the focus here is on the storyline and your activities, and I think it's quite fascinating. The devs did well, letting you browse websites, hack into chats, wiretap phones, hacking desktops. Sure, it will eventually feel a bit "on rails", as you basically look for bits marked in blue and upload them, progressing the story with that, and the relevant bits are the only ones you can use and upload... so the game kind of leads you by the hand. All you do is read and scroll, find the info, drag it to the upload queue. 

However... I do think that a) if you bother to read what is going on, it might actually make you think a bit, and b) the story is pretty interesting, and I can't wait to see where all this leads. Really like the periodic release... every week, there is a new episode, which you are being told about by email. 

In a nutshell - this is a rather interesting little game with some very cool ideas. It might make you think about the story, government involvement, whether the end always justifies the means, and you might ponder who is right and who is wrong in this story. 
There are some technical problems (for example, if you play this on two different devices, you might run into a problem with starting the game on one of them), but the devs are looking into any problem and are clearly communicating what is going on - nice job there. 

Bottom-line
Great little game, eager to see more of it. Quite a bit of reading involved, but this game will make you think, it's an interesting take on the whole idea of Big Brother is watching you, and is quite well executed. 

So far: 7.5/10, score will probably go up once more episodes are released

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What would you do if you really wanted to imprison some people that irked you? Obviously, you would scour their Facebook, Twitter, and eHarmony profiles to gather evidence of corroboration between them and terrorist activist cells. Atleast that’s how Osmotic Studios would do it. Although it may be a bit of a crude hyperbole, that is essentially what you will be doing in Orwell, the fascinating game where you play as Big Brother in an effort to keep The Nation safe and discover the culprits behind the recent bombing events in the capital city.

[h1]Privacy vs Security[/h1]

Other than being the author of 1984, the story where this game gets many of its motifs from, Orwell is rebirthed as a new governmental security program created to maintain order and reduce crime in a totalitarian country called, The Nation. Being an all-encompassing program with no bounds in breaking personal privacy, Orwell has the ability to retrieve: medical records, user submitted online information, bank statements, school records, mobile device data, telephone calls, chat room conversations, and pc device data. Your role in ensuring the safety of The Nation is in the capacity of an investigator, one who has authority to utilize the Orwell mainframe as an unbiased outsider to The Nation. As an investigator, you must sift through all of the information Orwell retrieves to discover and submit “relevant” datachunks to your immediate supervisor. What you deem relevant will shape the futures of the suspects under investigation, so take great care in deciding what to submit to Orwell.

Gameplay-wise, Orwell’s UI behaves much like an internet browser with three major utilities: the Reader, Listener, and Insider. These utilities allow you to pull up internet-related articles, tap into phone calls or chat conversations, or remote control mobile/PC devices respectively. Throughout the countless scripts of text provided by the articles or conversations, datachunks are automatically highlighted, and notifications beside specific entries where datachunks are present help guide the player towards progression. Some datachunks will be relatively useless, such as a person’s favorite color, but others will be extremely relevant to the case. Chunk by chunk, you will eventually develop fully-fleshed profiles to aid you in determining who the next person of interest is until the final culprit is found.

[h1]License to Know[/h1]

Using Orwell's features is the crux of the game, letting you slowly form your own opinion on who may be innocent or an accomplice, all while unraveling deeper motivations about the suspects and influential figures around you and Orwell. When you think you've cleanly profiled someone, post-incident reports will reveal multiple perspectives with conflicting beliefs that you may have never even thought of. As each episode focuses on a different character, everyone feels really well developed and sharply defined by disparate personalities and lifestyles. In addition, the more you learn about one thing, the less confident you will feel about another. 

Although the detective aspect of the game begins off strong, it unfortunately slowly undermines itself due to the fact that every clue is essentially hand-fed to the player. Since notifications of datachunks are provided, what ended up seeming to be a neat and helpful feature to ensure that I can progress without too much trouble began to feel like a massive crutch. This created an extremely casual playstyle where I was really just along for the ride. Don't get me wrong, it is still one great journey, but the immersiveness could have been kicked up a notch by providing players a serious investigative challenge. For example, if all notifications and highlighted entries were removed, it would definitely force me to care much more about the seemingly mundane or extraneous text for fear of relevancy. Finding the clues could be as "simple" as manually highlighting useful data. The supervisor continued to nag me about looking for X, finding X, learning more about X, but eventually the clues led me there without trying anyways. I felt like I might as well just speed-read anything without highlighted text in it to quickly move on. 

In addition, certain clues must be fed to Orwell to proceed, even if I wanted to exclude it. The game seems to make a big deal about being careful what to upload to the mainframe, so why force me to make choices like that. Maybe I'm inclined to believe X is innocent, but to proceed, I must upload information that X has a military background in order to create clearance for investigation. Having this feature further supports the casual mindset of submitting anything that is highlighted and diminishes the need to read everything or even care. Don’t get me wrong, the game still provides the players with a fair amount of control, since the endings are vastly different and minor paths will affect the outcome of certain suspects, but I definitely did not welcome the need to have milestone/checkpoint datachunks for progression.

The datachunk system still has some pretty neat features though, most notably in regards to data conflicts. At these moments, two conflicting statements are uncovered and only one can be submitted. You will essentially provide info that you want your supervisor to act upon. Ex. "I heard X was home last night....[phone conversation]" vs "Me and X had a blast at the concert last night [social networking site]." What you choose will relatively dictate what will happen to X. These conflicts returned a little bit of control taken away with the abovementioned checkpoint chunks.

[h1]Complete Walkthrough Playlist[/h1]

https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=s6Q75R9yWtU&list=PLeavCsRFiP55ATTks7hLjJY84dnSIXY3y&index=1

[h1]Verdict[/h1]

At first, Orwell seemed to have been just a more interactive visual novel or point & click game, but certain scripted scenes suddenly thrust me into Orwell's world, making me experience the exact same feelings a tech-savvy security investigator would be facing. Times where I would suddenly lose access to Orwell's mainframe, experience a cyber-attack, discover life-threatening secrets or aid Orwell during an active escape attempt. I found myself making motions and exasperations my virtual counterpart would most likely make, and the intense emotions I felt during these moments are something that would be highly difficult to forget as I walk away from the game. I can't recall any visual novels or point & clicks that have made me feel so involved in its world, seemingly shaping the final conclusion to the story.

Even though I have some gripes with Orwell’s progression and datachunk systems, the game is a far cry from being a failure at its attempt to tell a captivating story with novel methods. It isn’t easy for a game to present information in such a way to draw strong opinions from the players, yet manage to continually make their beliefs sway back and forth. The developers, however, knew how to create false trails, dead ends, probable causes and multiple motivations yet skew them towards a believable conclusion. Furthermore, scripted moments that nearly broke the fourth wall created a unique sense of immersion and relatability. This makes it very easy for me to recommend Orwell to any fan of story-centric narratives or spy games. If you’re still on the fence about this game, try the demo. It is free and contains the entire first episode - and it only gets better from there.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] An Excellent Educational Tool for Teaching People the Value of Privacy [/h1]

I am going to start this review with a hot take: people don't care much about privacy. At least not in the way we're taught to think about it. People desire privacy when they want to hide from others—especially people they know. A classic example of this is your average teenager concealing their sexual activity from their parents. We can define this as [b]interpersonal privacy[/b]—the need and right to keep parts of ourselves hidden from the people around us. In a limited sense, people do care about having (intepersonal) privacy  in their lives. 

But what about a faceless entity like a government agency or a big tech company? Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not.

Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided.

[list]
[*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it.
[*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens.
[*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list]

Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse.

Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy.

[h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1]

[h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2]
[list]
[*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women."
[*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps?
[*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps?
[*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism?
[/list]

If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have.

[h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2]
Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! 

This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy!

Bottom line:  I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth!

[h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2]
Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with.

That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him!

[h2] Reading Haters [/h2]
Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle.

My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts.

[h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2]
Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that.

[h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2]
The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%.

Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch!

My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements.

For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! 

[h1] Overall Rating [/h1]
[b] WIP, FIS, IIS
2+2=5/6 [/b]

Should we seek privacy from their probing eyes? Do we even deserve the right to privacy from the government and Big Tech? This is precisely where people will shrug their shoulders and say that they don't understand or care. Interpersonal privacy matters to the common man. Privacy from institutions and systems does not. Why are we like this? The reasons for this range from the righteous to the fearful to the misguided. [list] [*] Fear: A citizen concerned for their safety will give up essential liberty as Ben Franklin pointed out. This was evident after the Patriot Act was passed. It was evident again after the Snowden leaks. People feel like they will be safe from violent crime if they give up rights. As Franklin rightly noted, this safety is but temporary. It is futile to give up your rights to secure it. [*] Righteousness: Many people use the 'nothing to hide' fallacy to justify the lack of privacy. People will say that they are not criminals. And so, they have nothing to hide from the government. This righteousness is misguided because it is based on the presumption that governments are always righteous and have the best intentions for their subjects. Governments can and do turn tyrannical—when they do, they spy on and punish citizens. [*] Ignorance (of consequence): People do not understand how much private information the government and BIg Tech has about them. Information is power—this is especially true in the age of data. Information about you can be used to easily understand and manipulate you. But people do not understand how private information is collected and misused. And so they don't care about privacy. [/list] Educating people about the need for, let alone the right to privacy is a challenging task. We need to reframe and redirect the conversation away from interpersonal privacy to privacy from insitutions. Doing this is difficult because institutional surveillance feels like an abstract concept to many. This is precisely where the game Orwell excels. Osmotic Studios does a great job of showing why your life should be private from the government and Big Tech. In Orwell, you play as a government agent snooping on ordinary citizens. You gather personal information for a surveillance system designed to store data and weaponize it. Every piece of information you harvest is used to create damaging narratives, justify injustice and enable tyranny. The net result of your gameplay is acutely felt on a personal level. Your actions lead to individuals being maligned, families torn apart and the world becoming worse. Orwell is thus a great educational tool for privacy advocates looking to teach the public about the value of and the right to privacy. [h1] Recommendations for Specific Gamers [/h1] [h2] Voyeuristic & Paranoid Gamers [/h2] [list] [*] Do you lie in bed with your partner, look at him and think to yourself: "I bet he's thinking about other women." [*] Do you spy on your loving girlfriend's phone because you constantly suspect her of using dating apps? [*] Are you a chai enthusiast who loves to talk about tea with other women on Tea apps? [*] Or perhaps you are a masculine married man who revels in the simple joys of candaulism? [/list] If you answered yes to any of these questions, you must play Orwell! The game is a voyeur's delight. It will scratch every voyeuristic itch—and trust issues—that you have. [h2] Gamers Who Love to Gaslight & Manipulate [/h2] Orwell not only allows you to spy on people but also to shape the narrative about them. Do you want a woman to be seen as a loving single mom who dotes on her child? Or do you want her to be seen as a mentally unstable terrorist who commits violence? You have the power to choose in Orwell! This ability to manipulate and shape narratives is one of the best gameplay mechanics in Orwell. You can gaslight the government itself into believing what you want them to believe! Wonderful! This is exactly why video games appeal to the male fantasy! Bottom line: I cared too much about getting things right while playing Orwell. But the game doesn't want you to do that! In fact, creating a false narrative about NPC characters is required for some achievements. So yeah, don't worry too much. Go ahead and play fast and loose with the truth! [h2] 1984 Enjoyers [/h2] Let's get this straight: Orwell is a great tool to teach people about privacy. But it is no literary masterpeice. Yes the game pays homage to 1984. But Orwell treads familiar ground about liberty, security and privacy. It is not designed to be a sophisticated commentary on the issues and concepts it deals with. That said, I loved the character of Abraham Goldfels. He is a fascinating case study of a person who is co-opted by the very surveillance state he is trying to fight. Abraham is a complicated character with ambiguous motivations. I started the game feeling a sense of admiration for his intellectual nature and ability to lead. I ended the game feeling conflicted about his past and his life choices. What do you think of Abraham? Leave a message in the comments sections if you'd like to talk about him! [h2] Reading Haters [/h2] Orwell is a text heavy game. You will be reading and analyzing articles, chat logs, documents, emails and much more. For those who love reading books, Orwell is an enjoyable game. But those who dislike reading will struggle. My eyes did sometimes glaze over the many walls of text I went through. Fortuntately, the plot and gameplay is engaging enough to sustain you through. The first episode feels sluggish as you learn the ropes of the game. But keep at it: Orwell gets a lot more interesting in the later acts. [h2] Atmospheric Music Enjoyers [/h2] Orwell's soundtrack is definitely vibey. The slow and atmospheric music gets you in the mood of being a detective who is investigating criminal cases. Not a music critic so I can't say more than that. [h2] Achievement/Completionist Hunters [/h2] The game is not too hard for achievement hunters and completionists. Multiple playthroughs are not needed. You only need to replay some episodes to get specific achievements. I recommend [url=https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=907778579] using this achievement guide [/url] which helped me get 100%. Warning: Orwell is buggy and suffers from major save file issues. Backing up game files will not help IMO because of the persistent autosave feature. The first time I played Orwell, I lost progress and so I quit playing. The second time around, I finished the game and then bounced between chapters to get the remaining achievements. Once again, the game tripped up and asked me to replay the game from scratch! My advice is to play through the game once. Then check which achievements you need and which episodes they fall in. Need achievements for Episodes 4 & 5? Replay [b] those episodes first in chronological order [/b]. If necessary, repeat the episodes until you get all the episode specific achievements. For Episodes 1-3, I recommend creating a [b] separate profile [/b] and then playing the episodes in order. Episode 3 in particular is a mess because you have to replay it 3 times at least to get the achievements! [h1] Overall Rating [/h1] [b] WIP, FIS, IIS 2+2=5/6 [/b]

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Unfortunately I didn't enjoy Orwell at all. Admittedly, it's been a sponatenous purchase, done out of sheer curiosity to see what the fuzz is all about.

But instead of a dystopian thriller, blending story and gameplay together with an innovative user interface, I got quite a dull experience.

Actually Orwell isn't a game at all, it's rather a semi-interactive story which simply progresses together with the text snippets you highlight  ("upload"). To make things a bit more interesting, your fictional self is supposed to participate in a surveillance and data mining program which observes persons and evaluates their behavior. You do that by browsing through social media profiles, reading blogs, newspapers, looking at photos and following text chats.

Noticed something? Yes, it's basically down to reading. The whole game could have been perfectly realized via a website, there is basically only a minimal amount of graphic assets involved. Now while that might work out for a well written game, it unfortunately fails for Orwell.

The story line tries to explore the important question of privacy, civil liberties and how social media and data mining can lead to their erosion, especially in light of an ubiqitous fear of terrorist acts.

But whoever wrote Orwell did it so heavy-handedly, that you quickly feel like you're stuck in a school lesson, with the teacher dancing around the obvious answer, because he thinks it's too complicated for you to understand it right away.

Even worse, while you might even find the person you follow being an interesting character, making you feel invested in how your actions will affect their life, you are constantly delayed by the process of gathering key information which will trigger the next story snippet.

And no, it's not interesting to browse through some fictional website, filled with trite and shallow pseudo-philosophical ramblings, in order to find that little piece of incriminating information which will suddenly prompt your supervisor to announce the next story progress ("she's a suspect, let's wiretap her / she's guilty, I am sending in the force with an arrest warrant). 

Actually it's quickly making you search for the next key snippet, dragging it to the upload window, just to rinse and repeat with another source you'll be presented with.

So bottom line, while playing Orwell I wondered what I am actually doing here.

If I want to have a linear story, presented (mainly) via text, guess what? Yes, I'll read a book. The benefit of doing so is that it's very probably better written, more accessible and I don't need to stare at a screen.

If I want to play a game, I will play a game. But then I expect something to actually utilize the manifold ways of presenting a story and of including me, the player (not reader), in its progress. (And yes, I actually play some classic text-adventure now and then.)

Orwell is neither the first nor the latter. It's an experiment which seems to aim high, but soon falls flat in its core design. After an hour I had enough. I'm not feeling invested or intrigued to continue at all, so Orwell will join the forbidden crypt of mistakes somewhere in the forsaken depths of my library.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Pros:
- Art style is interesting and engaging
- Story is well crafted and immersive
- Exposition isn't forced on you, but it is there if you wish to learn more about the world or certain characters
- Creators clearly spent a lot of time and effort on the setting 
- The game tackles some pretty engaging ethical dilemas that are applicable to the world we live in

Cons:
- Click and drag simulator 2016
- Uninspired gameplay mechanics 
- Constant handholding (I kept thinking I was in a long tutorial but that's just how the game is)
- Very binary choices (he did it vs she did it/ she did the right thing vs she is bad)
- No real detective work the game just tells you everything
- The game treats you like an idiot by having a sidekick tell you what each piece of info means


Other things that bothered me:

-      Chat/phone calls move too fast to keep up with uploading the 'chunks' that appear and you're forced to either ignore the dialogue progression and try to click on a certain chuck as the screen constantly shifts or wait until the exchange is  done to upload anything (or maybe I was just too slow).

-      Music shifts in tone dramtically whenever 'shocking info' is revealed which makes the game feel very linear (which it is) instead of just letting you stumble upon the info yourself and make your own conclusions as to what is important. The music changes give the feeling of "This was a scripted event that I experienced at a designated time."

-      Your partner/boss just tells you things so you don't really have to do any investigation yourself which is kind the whole point of the game. 

-      You are fed information in a pretty constant chronological stream instead being given all the info at once and having to sort through it with your brain. The game treats you like a baby and doesn't give you your next treat until you click and drag the things on the page it just gave you. 

-      The game established this rhythm really early of scrolling through a page, clicking on stuff, listening to your buddy pal guy tell you stuff, being given a new page, then repeating.

-      The fact that the chats/calls don't start until you actively bring them up is quite harmful to immersion (why would the people wait to start talking on the phone for 5 seconds until I'm monitoring them? Just have them act like normal humans and not wait for the player).

-      The gameplay would be a lot better if the events driving the characters weren't so close to the present. If we as players were given this new technology to help solve a crime in the past (several months at least) it would eliminate the need to have these awfully convenient text conversations and phone calls every 5 seconds that always have important info. What I'm saying is put the event in the past so that the player can be given a bunch of call transcripts and chat logs to sift through instead of being handed the info.

-      The very nature of how the game highlights all of the important info for you makes you question what your job really is and why anyone would need you to do it. If they already have a system that determines what is important and human operators who interpret the data (your boss/partner guy), why the hell do they need you???

-      The info highlighting eventually has you just scrolling through pages until something lights up or you get an update instead of actually reading the page and deciding what is important and what is irrelevant.




This is not a bad game by any means. It's just always frustrating when I see one of these "choices matter" games where there's clearly a certain path you're encouraged to take and you really aren't free to do things your own way.

While I had pretty high expectations for this game after coming off a Hacknet binge, I just feel as though the game is trying to pretend to be something it's not. Just market the game for what it is, a linear narrative experience.

I'm very aware that since I did not finish the game my perspective is limited to what I played, but what I played I did not enjoy, so I cannot reccomend this game.

TL;DR: This game is a very and hand-holdy linear story based experience while it is advertised to be a sort of detective

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I just finished this game. I like many of the latest reviews received this as part of a humble bundle. Unlike many of the reviewers I am no stranger to the concept of interactive fiction. As such I cannot say "WOW so unique." This game has many elements I found fascinating, and indeed I played through the whole thing in one go, a very do-able task. I think there are many things that would make me recommend it, but there are two glaring holes that I think bring it just shy of a general recommendation. I can say this, If you have never played an interactive fiction game, and the plot sounds intriguing, buy it. It is worth ten dollars. If you got it in a humble bundle or something similar, play it. You will have an entertaining few hours. If you do not fall in to either of those two camps I would recommend a pass. 

The good - 
Plot- Everything to do with the plot is great. The characters are interesting, and they do to some degree develop. The world feels complete and well rounded, The plot is where this game shines, as it should be as interactive fiction lives and dies by the plot. 
The interface - For the most part is pretty solid. There are few idiosyncrasies. The one glaring hole is the need for a few hot-keys, if only Enter and ESC, would make this much easier on the wrists, but it is as a whole soundly usable. 

The bad - For the bad I will go in to detail as to hopefully explain my point of view fully to the Devs.  There is at least one more season planned, and I would love to play it. Perhaps the Devs will hear this feedback and consider it. Before I continue though, if you have already thought “I kinda want to play this game,” do it and forget the ramblings of an old gamer. 

Choice - If the plot is what an interactive fiction game lives and dies by then choice (or for that matter the illusion of choice) is what allows it to breath. In Orwell the idea of choice dies very quickly, and never returns. There are several pivotal moments which finds the player, through the narrative, put in a position to make a pivotal choice. All the relevant characters are obviously pointing at you and saying you decide. I never really felt like there was any choices to be made. Either The player is not given enough context to understand the consequences of that choice, in these cases you are just blindly choosing one of two options and made to accept the consequences. Or you cannot progress until you make the choice. 

At the heart of this, in my opinion, is the engine for which you as the player progress through the narrative. You are told at the very beginning of the game that you cannot progress until you have uploaded certain information. Which pieces of information allows for progression is up to the game. The premise of games like this in which it is up to the player to provide or not provide information to the antagonist is a great juxtaposition to make the player feel invested, and in many cases responsible for the consequences levied on the characters in the narrative. Games like “Papers Please” and “Beholder” levy this mechanic very well. In Orwell you cannot progress without giving the Antagonist certain information. This kills the illusion of choice, and make the rest of the narrative lose it's bite. Because I cannot NOT provide certain information the consequences are not my fault. The game made me do it. Especially in those moments where you have several data points you can give, and you need to choose between them, but if you choose wrong the game does not go forward, you end up throwing whatever data points at the wall, even those bits of data you do not want to provide, in order to get the game to continue. 

I realize why it was written this way. You cannot write a narrative which has ALL possibilities. So in order to move forward you need the player to trip certain triggers. An elegant way around this in my opinion would be to allow the information to be presented in "real time." This allows the narrative to continue while allowing the player more of a choice in the way it unfolds. I think this would greatly improve the impact of the game. 

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) 
If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned.


There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. 

Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, 
"Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." 
and this narrative missed that promise.

The Twist - (mild spoiler warning) If you have read this far then I doubt this will really be a spoiler, but just in case, you have been warned. There is a twist at the end. All good who-done-it's have them. This is no exception. My issue with the twist at the end of Orwell dove tails in to the idea of choice. There is no way you the player, let alone the character you play in the game, could predict it. There are no data points that I found that will allow you to discover the twist in game. Therefore it feels arbitrary. Once again the narrative loses impact because it does not feel like the player could intercede. The game is going to do what it is going to do and you are just pulled along to see what happens. that is what novels, TV shows, movies, and comic books are for. In fact I could see this story being a great Rashamon-Style comic, but as an interactive fiction I think this game falls flat. Summery - In summation I think if you are interested in games as an art form, or are just curios about what happens in this particular narrative, then this is worth while. I look forward to see if any of these issues are fixed in the next chapter. I do not regret my time "playing" this game. but I think in the end, The impact of the events was greatly blunted by the mechanics with which the narrative is presented. That seems a shame to me as the story could be quit impact-full if only the illusion of choice was maintained through out. In a narrative the promise of the premise is key, "Only the information you provide will be seen by the security forces and acted upon. You decide what gets seen and what does not, influencing how the suspects will be perceived." and this narrative missed that promise.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Orwell is a fresh new take on the visual novel game format. The game UI immediately immerses the player, placing you squarely in the driver seat as you try to unravel a bombing plot and pursue justice... but for whom?[/h1]

[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
You take on the role of a government surveillance cyber-investigator. Your task is to get into a person’s life through their social media, bank accounts, phone taps and chat messages. Drag and drop important bits of information (data chunks) into the ORWELL interface to upload these bits of data to form dossiers and help your supervisor inform the local authorities. 

[h1]PROS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Evocative Experience[/u][/b]: 
Almost immediately, you’ll be oriented into the role of a cyber surveillance investigator and the stakes don’t get much higher than trying to unravel a terrorist plot. This game will make you *[b]feel[/b]* things and think about morality. 

[*][b][u]Novel UI [/u][/b]:
I think the UI is definitely the best part of the game, as it is designed in such a way to evoke the feeling of using some official piece of government software. Most of your interactions are in the form transcribed phone conversations, chat logs and browsing “online” content. 

[*][b][u]Art Style[/u][/b]:
The pixelated, somewhat-cartoony photos of people and places creates the perfect balance of reality and surreality. Probably for the best, as the game’s primary focus is to get you thinking about the heavy moral issues related to a surveillance society, as depicted by the game’s very Orwellian world. 

[*][b][u]Music[/u][/b]: Almost invisible, but ever present, the music stylings accented the drama perfectly. 
[/list]

[h1]CONS:[/h1]
[list]
[*][b][u]Lack of Visual Information[/u][/b]: 
A significant part of this game is reading text. Which you then choose to upload to Orwell or ignore (depending on the context of the circumstances and your personal value system).  

However, there were several times when I literally could not continue the game because the next event had to be triggered by me uploading some [b][u]some very specific, but unknown[/u][/b] piece of data. This created a situation where I would upload more info than I wanted to, just in an effort to trigger the next cutscene. 

Rather than guessing, it would have been nice if the designers could have implemented a color system or some other way to indicate what data was tied to progressing the story. I suppose the current implementation is more true to life, but it lessened my sense of agency when I would upload some seemingly innocuous data and suddenly my supervisor would dm me with a new break in the case. 

[*][b][u]File Organization[/u][/b]: 
By the end of the game, there are dozens of pages of fictitious files and documents to sift through... and the game did NOT make that task much easier. Could I get some bookmarks, please?

[*][b][u]RAILROADING[/u][/b]: 
So, I won’t say much here out of respect for spoilers, but suffice it to say that the design choices made in the game make it very clear how the developers feel regarding the subject matter. This bias in design limited the scope of user choice and the kinds of endings you can get. It would have been very interesting to have a greater variety of outcomes. It would have also worked to underscore the sense of user agency that they’d worked so hard to create in the first place.

[*][b][u]Short Length [/u][/b]: 
I’ve finished 2 complete playthroughs at 11 hours... which, given the minimalism of the graphics, seems extremely short and makes the current price of $9.99 a bit pricey.
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
Overall a very interesting and unique experience that I mostly enjoyed. However, because of the political nature of the game and the railroading embedded by the developers, I don’t think I’ll be buying any DLC any time soon, nor would I recommend the game at its current price of $9.99.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
"War is peace.
Freedom is slavery.
Ignorance is strength."

It is one of the most notable quotes from a breathtaking dystopian novel George Orwell's 1984 about totalitarian government. It's also one of my favorite novels of all time and it introduced me to dystopian genre in literature. Some people said 1984 was a self-fulfilling prophecy because government now can keep an eye on their people much easier thanks to technology. They can read your e-mails, chats, watch your moves through cameras, and probably know who you are.

Even if there's cryptography can encrypt our data, I sometimes think that privacy is still a myth.

Only a few minutes in, I'm already hooked to this game. We were 'chosen' to be a controller of Orwell system in order to maintain peace and security in a city. You're given access to read news, websites, someone's e-mails account, private chats, record calls, and even read someone's bank transaction. Unfortunately, there was a bomb explosion that killed citizens and we must find the real culprit based on the data we've got. But, do the data really tell us the truth? Or are we not capable enough to distinguish which one is the truth and which one is a lie?

2 + 2 = 5

(Full review coming soon after I finished playing all of the episodes.)

review_text_raw:
Picked this gem up today and im quite impressed. I do have some issues with it but all in all im pleased with the purchase.
other comments have done an excellent job of explaining the game and a quick youtube video of the first few minutes was all i needed to buy the game so i wont go into that. 

HOWEVER i do want to hand out my current gripes with the game in hopes that future games wont follow in the same lines. in my opnion some of the choices that conflict are just down right nonsense. Ill do my best not to spoil but jesus i just came a HUGE plot point where my two options were both (in my opnion) equally important and worth noting but you can only choose one so here i go picking the one i figured was slightly more "right" than the other..... i was not only wrong but horribly wrong costing peoples lives. In my opnion BOTH of those point should have been checked atleast mentioned but they werent and it really broke the atmosphere for me. suddenly i wasn't the detective hunting baddies and avoiding bullshit and speculation, i was now some moron unable to take notes on two important details in a major case........ 

Now in fairness, thusfar, thats only happened once but sadly its not all. Ive come across information that groups two or three facts together into one choice or situations where i didn't feel like that view point i was forced to choose was correct in some cases and it hurt my feelings for the case as a whole. On and on theres choices i don't really feel like they work or that information is looked over by my character or the machine thing and its just really sad becasue the game is amazing and then i get yanked out of the world becasue a choice is way off from my view point.

Again i appologize for being so vague and i WISH i could discuss the actual choices ive mentioned here becasue without playing it they may not make sense to everyone..... however i dont want to spoil anything in this game becasue even when i dislike a choice or view the game itself is just fantastic. well worth the $10 for it and im certainly looking forward to completing and honestly a next game lol. 

TLDR: Great game, has some story flaws (my personal opnion doesn't reflect everyones view) but well worth the $10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL is a hybrid game somewhere between visual novel and point and click adventure. In the game, you are an investigator hired by the nation in testing out a new law which allows the government to spy on its citizens in order to find criminals. While this doesn’t sound too far off from where we are today, we can assume ordinary citizens aren’t having their wires tapped and all their online activity personally searched into. But that blurred line between what in this game is fiction and what is potential reality is where the game really shines, and pushes me to giving this game a general recommendation.
ORWELL starts off with investigating into a bomb that went off on a popular plaza and investigating a person of interest who was at the plaza. This is the only cutscene in the game and I really need to say that it shows how ugly the art style is. ORWELL has this odd polygonal art style that just doesn’t look right, and the game does nothing to utilize the style as well. Take a game like Wind Waker and the cell shading is important to the overall feel of the game, and the entire game would be very different if they had gone in a more realistic style. ORWELL does not earn that right to have an abstract art style, and it looks all the worse because of it. 
After the explosion, you begin digging into the meat of the game, which is going through people’s internet presence and phone calls and finding condemning information about them to fit them for the crime. The writing here then would be the important aspect to take away, and getting generally invested in the world or ORWELL should take precedence. However, this is another place where if the world of ORWELL was given to another developer with another vision, it probably would’ve been much more successful in world building that ORWELL currently is. The characters all generally fall into 2 categories; people who rebel against the government and people who are roped into rebelling against the government, and as such you get a lot of “it’s us or big brother vibes” when making your decisions which tends to not make the decisions feel organic. At several points in the game you can choose whether to report certain information to your supervisor and it affects how the supervisor views the target. However, these choices are often obviously superficial, and the contrasting information that you can give is usually contradicting in the sense that some information is outdated while other information is up to date. This is different than what an actual Orwellian inspired piece would aim for, where there are 2 facts that cannot exist within the same space and you are forced to accept both. For example, one contrasting information you need to choose between uploading to your supervisor is someone’s address. One is obviously right, and the other is outdated. It doesn’t mean the person didn’t use to previously live at the outdated address, but it’s just a matter of relevance. The game would be cooler if there were more instances of actual “doublethink” moments, instead of relying on portraying certain information in a correct or incorrect way. 
Speaking of being more Orwellian, the world of ORWELL is loaded with references to the novel by George Orwell, 1984. But this is another reason why the experience of the game is cheapened. A lot of the characters in the game are obvious references to people in 1984 and other dystopian media, such as a friend named Huxley or using the screenname w1n5t0n. If done sparingly, this could’ve been a neat little nod to the works of Orwell, but literally every character you interact with has some connection to the book, and the writing again suffers. It’s no longer a “hey, that’s a pretty neat reference,” but more so a “none of these characters seem original because the source material is being way overused.”
Ok, so all I’ve done is talk about the bad art style, the lacking writing, and non-significance of the gameplay, so why would I still recommend it? The reason I recommend it is because of that blurred line I mentioned at the beginning. That feel where you feel like you are gathering information about just another ordinary citizen, your mind begins to go what would this world really be like? If I send this review to my friends on messenger, what could someone get from my writing of it? One of the other things that happens a lot in the game is the people you talk to get implicated as well, so if I sent a message saying I was planning an attack to my group of friends, in ORWELL, everyone would be investigated on to find more evidence behind my potential crime and if they were involved in anyway. I think when some paths lead nowhere in ORWELL, it’s only a natural consequence that not everyone is going to be a criminal in the eyes of the government, but following the path to the end is pretty satisfying in the game. Despite the lackluster writing and world building, you do actually feel a voyeuristic guilt looking into everyone life between their social media accounts, medical records, college attendance, job records, blog posts, and so on. You can’t help but think if someone were to investigate me, they would find my screennames, my posts all over the internet, my video replays from streaming, and could trace words I said years ago to implicate me in something I was not a part of.
Altogether, the game has obvious flaws. It’s short, it has a forgettable art style, forgettable characters, and overall a forgettable plot. But playing through everything and seeing how everything plays out is thrilling in a way that no other game has ever provided for me. There is an ORWELL season 2 planned, and if they could just step away from the source material and feel more liberty to explore the world they’ve gone ahead and made, a lot of the issues I have with season 1 would be rectified. Overall, a 7/10. If you like dystopian media and the thought be being a voyeur into the lives of the ordinary citizens, give it a shot.

review_text_raw:
I believe Fellow Traveller Games is very interested in making people switch to Tails with giving away their published "Linux basics" game Hacknet for free (multiple times even!) first, and now give away this game too to fuel your paranoia and use some of that know-how to make you try and hide.

Tin foil hat aside, here's a proper review;

First a little disclaimer, not recommended if you use a monitor smaller than 1080p, especially if you have an unusual aspect ratio too.
The font in some spots looks terrible, occasionally skipping through thinner letters like i's and l's altogether and overall making the rest harder to read, notably the whole TNB stuff aside the headlines.
There is no way to change the font neither through options nor through config files, forum searches gave nothing in regards to that either, so be mindful of that.

Firstly this is a visual novel, so no super exciting and engaging gameplay is to be found, but honestly that may be for the better in these spying games.

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story.
But if you like these spying games and want one focused on gameplay, go and check out Beholder instead.

Otherwise if a more streamlined experience suits you better, proceed with this review.
Firstly, I'm not a Visual Novel expert, this one is my first one that wasn't completely linear, so the bar was set very low with the few ones I've played being just click proceed until all of the text scrolls past. Well this one has proper branching patchs and dfferent endings and little optional side stuff too. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough.

You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three.
You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel.
At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue.

Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc.

I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot.
But turns out the sequel actually plays alongside the original with focus on that foreign affairs story with the bombings plot of the original serving as a backdrop helping you keep track of the time.

Overall I'd say the game is fun, you won't get more than 18 hours out of it even if you 100% it, so I don't know at what price you should get it if you missed he free promo.
The sequel seems promising though, and there's also the whole movie shooting actor/director feud in the news much like the war, so trilogy potential?

I have played a little bit of Beholder and the more involving gameplay was a huge turn off due to how boring the whole manually keep track of data part already is, and Beholder also puts you on a timer and penalizes you for messing up by submitting wrong data for the whole accountant simulator part, and that is not counting the other gameplay aspects like resource management, relationships with people and quests and the overall keeping track of who is where part in the house sections. Even though I usually play famously difficult games on at least Normal mode and the others on at least Hard, if I get back to that one I'll play it on Easy because I find it too dull to even bother sitting through to get the story. Although one part in the middle is tipped a lot into one outcome where one misclick or two can invalidate the other two. Achievement wise it is basically confirmed to be that way sice the common outcome is almost the same rarity as the completion of the respective chapter, the rarer outcome being the rarest achievement in the game and the middle one still being rare. I didn't like how rigged that was, trying to do it differently on another playthrough got me back to the same outcome eventually having me use a guide in a third playthrough. You basically just have to drag and drop images and blue and yellow highlighted text to play the game, blue usually you don't worry too much just trying to ignore the obvious lies and for yellow, find the correct one of of two or three. You don't have time and upload count pressure for MOST of the game, something being much different in the sequel. At least with the highlighted text processing huge amount of data isn't a nightmare, just scroll through that wall of text of names in a list until dramatic music starts playing and the important stuff glows blue. Some other quirks, this seems far less fleshed out gameplay mechanics wise than what I saw of the first 30 mins of the sequel. No voice acting for phone calls, lack of proper passage of time, less input options for the player etc. I was disappointed when the achievement Win the War was not about the whole tensions between countries situation you're reading about in the news on the side of the main plot. review_text_raw:
I really enjoyed Papers, Please.  I really enjoyed Beholder.  The "authoritarian minion simulator" is a really interesting game concept, and I wanted to like it, but Orwell just bored me.

It should be picking up clues to things that should go together, but gameplay is all highlighted drag & drop.  And thus I found myself not really caring.

It doesn't help that the drag & drop simulated internet is just enough of a facsimile to remind me I could be doing this on the real internet and it would be easier (albeit dead internet making it slightly harder in 2026).

You could quite literally start an X account and start reading posts by (let's see if my review makes it to being posted now!) Nick Shirley about mass fraud in the US or Rupert Lowe about mass... problems... in the UK and look for crimes actually being committed or covered up, then go and look at the names/places/groups in the reports they put out and start doing your own investigative work and start posting publicly available but little-known connections as you find them... and it would be both meaningful and less boring.  You wouldn't be an authoritarian minion, you'd just be someone doing basic investigative citizen journalism (or wonky tisming), but it's just finding connections.  Every "this you?" tweet where someone researches a political/celebrity timeline to find contradictory positions is more interesting that Orwell.

And that's why Orwell is weak.  Rather than go "huh, what's out there", it prompts the next link on a fake web, with things to drag and drop, over and over.

I wanted to like it, but found the story not hooking me in, the gameplay a tedious, railroading copy of the real internet, and overall just bleh.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Given all the positive reviews, I thought Orwell would be a more interesting game than it actually is.
But the gameplay is mostly boring. In a way, it is very similar to a text-adventure game. You read through/listen to all the documents given access to (webpages, chat sessions or phone calls). But there is basically no investigative work, hacking or anything that would be fun to do to find information. All the work is already done for you, every document is already analyzed, and you cannot investigate new people before being allowed to, even if it is clear they must have some role in the investigation.

So yes, the gameplay is overly simple and very linear, but maybe I could have been ok with it if I had found the story interesting.
But the story is boring. The main goal in the game (at least until I stopped playing) is to find the culprits responsible for a bomb attack. Sounds exciting right? Except most of the info you have to read through is about the different suspects boring life, relationships and habits, things I don't give a damn about. So I guess this game is not for me.

Maybe the game becomes more complex and interesting later on (I really hope so), but I am just not interested enough so far in the story to continue playing. Maybe I'll try again later...

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game is so-so; I want to recommend something *like* Orwell, but I'm on the fence about recommending Orwell itself. The game raises interesting issues, and the world would indeed be better off if everyone had at least the simulated experience of working with a large-scale surveillance system. I even usually found the story compelling, and I finished the game. However, the execution also felt a little disappointing.

The main gameplay problem, in my experience, was that sometimes I felt forced to take random or stupid-seeming actions just to see what it was that would finally advance the plot. This was in spite of the "handholding" cues the game uses to help you along.

Another thing that bothered me was a set of accuracy/realism concerns, which I will go on about below.

*************************************************

(Optional section about accuracy)

My main objection is that the game gives a poor sense of what doing an investigation with help of an Orwell-like system would actually be like in real life. In real life, either A) the computer would be a very powerful autonomous system and would make conclusions without human or involvement; or B) the human researcher would have sensible basic capabilities such as updating information, correcting machine-extracted snippets, and supplementing files with written analysis. The game tries to be somewhere in between, and in the process makes something that's unrealistic and sometimes annoying.  Also, there were also moments of "what the heck does the game want from me now", when I would add pointless or even incorrect information to the Orwell database solely to see if it would finally be the thing to move the plot forward.

The fact that you can't modify information in the Orwell crime database is pretty stupid on the face of things. To be fair, though, maybe it stands metaphorically for problems that could actually arise. For example, if two government agencies had a file on you, but the two were not in sync, the fact that you're not actually a criminal could be updated in one department's file without the second department learning about this, and perhaps the second database could lead to your extrajudicial killing.

The contextless, overaly literal way that information is passed from investigator to police is completely absurd. Perhaps this is a useful reflection of one possible way that an agency using an Orwell-type system could be dysfunctionally structured, though you'd hope that a bureaucracy wouldn't be quite that stupid. Or perhaps this limited information passing is symbolic of a potentially problem where two crime databases were linked, but could only communicate back and forth using a limited, contextless technical vocabulary, which would perpetuate misunderstanding. 

Perhaps the point of the game, though, is not to be right about the *particulars* of what could go wrong in a mass surveillance system, but more to give people an accessible experience that gives a general sense of creepiness.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I can't imagine the replayability will be very high, but -- the premise of this game is both great and also very important. Working as a covert tech obtaining info publicly available online in order to put together information on suspects/targets can help shed light on just how much personal information is readily available on almost all people this day and age-- even this review. With due diligence, one can find tons of info on just about anyone. It freaks a lot of people out and seeing a Blue's Clue's version (closest analogy I could think of, game is not much like Blues Clues) might help ameliorate that. A popular tactic of authorities of any sort (hiring managers, law enforcement, parents, whatever) is to comb through someone's social media profile. -- and yet apparently people are still taken aback when someone finds and looks through their facebook profile. 

Anyway... this game addresses a lot of currently important social issues in an engaging and thought-provoking way. It's unique and fun and somehow manages this with being almost entirely text-based.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is engrossing and more than a bit disturbing considering the implications of some very real things that are happening in the world right now. More of an interactive novel than a proper game, it nonetheless pulled me in for the 3-4 hours it took to reach the end of it, as well as a couple of replays to try out different paths.

It's not perfect, though; there's no challenge in actually getting the information you require since it's highlighted for you and you simply have to upload it, which sort of takes most of the initiative out of your hands. You do get to decide how certain characters are viewed based on how much you pass on to the powers that be, and your choices affect how they're treated and what happens to them, but the prevailing narrative is more or less canned, on-rails, and you can't do very much to affect how it plays out other than within a narrow scope. Some of the decisions you make do have very profound consequences for the individuals concerned, and the first time through I did have a few things I deeply regretted because of what happened as a result.


The biggest downside is that the game is short and fairly linear; there are only so many branches/possibilties to explore, so once you've exhausted them, there's really not much replay value. 

I've seen a few comparisons made to Papers, Please, which is less slick to play but rather more profound to actually experience because of the huge number of variations in how it can go. Orwell comparatively lacks depth, but because you spend more time with all the characters and get to know them better (since you're snooping through their gadgets and availing yourself of some very personal details of their lives), what happens to them matters a lot more to you. At least, it mattered more to me. In Papers Please I was more concerned with getting myself and my family out of dodge. 

Think of Orwell as an interactive dystopian techno-thriller and you've got a pretty good idea what you're in for.

As an agent, you are privy to the entirety of your target’s posts, articles, phone calls, emails, etc. Use this information to reveal more and more relevant webpages and conversations. The catch? You’re overlooked by a supervisor and you must choose what information to upload. This supervisor can only see the bits of information you feed him, so choose wisely or risk ruining an innocent’s life. The challenge? Upload only enough information to gain new leads, but not jump to conclusions. 

Are you really helping the greater good by invading the privacy of the few? Or have you caused more harm than good, muddling in affairs you should have never been in? Are the internet spies of today, really the superheroes of tomorrow? Find out by stepping into these large, cyber shoes. Act quickly and stop a harmful event in its tracks, or wait it out and discover it was a false alarm. Big brother is watching you. You are watching the people. Lives are on the line. Decide. 

Then watch as you say, [b]“I never meant for this to happen.”[/b]

Let me start off this review by saying I’m one who really enjoys a story-based game. I particularly enjoy consequence based story games (like [i]Telltale[/i]). If that’s not your cup of tea, this game is not for you. If you’re still interested, here’s the pros and cons for the game so far.

[h1]Pros:[/h1] [b]Interesting social commentary.[/b] There’s no denying that this is the age of technology, and with that comes a whole new slew of problems that our forefathers never could have foresaw when drafting the constitution. [i]Orwell[/i] heavily and obviously alludes to the current hot topics of freedom of internet access, government access to our personal files and correspondences, and general cyber security we see crop up in the news time and time again. 

[b]Easy interface.[/b] There’s not much to learn but drag and drop. Your un-uploaded data chunks are marked so you don’t lose track of what you’ve read, need to read, and are saving for later.

[b]More unique game flow.[/b] Events don’t happen unless you upload data chucks, leaving you to explore the branches of plot in whatever order feels natural to you. It does still feel a bit restricted, though, (see “A bit linear, limited” in cons) a perhaps more of a pseudo-free-directional choice. (But isn’t the concept of freedom what this game is all about?) 

[b]Intriguing artwork.[/b] The geometric artistic style lends itself to unconsciously nod its head towards the cyber-oriented world of the game. It ties in beautifully to the theme of the game—from the logo to the interface—without being too aggressive.

[h1]Cons:[/h1] [strike][b]A better save system!![/b][/strike] Update has added a rewind system, but I have not played since [strike]I cannot stress this enough. Since this is a consequence-based game, I’d like to be able to start from the end episode one, or so, with my decisions staying the same, and only make changes to my decisions from there out, with my profiles branching out from my first play through plot line. Starting over from the beginning is too much of a grind. Even a way to speed up messaging/call text on the second (and beyond) playthrough would be better for acheivement hunters or people just curious about the other endings. Also, it’s glaringly obvious which pieces of text carry great significance. (Those will be the ones with conflicting evidence) so sometimes the challenge of deciding to report information right away or wait was quite discernible, offering no challenge. Although, I will say that there are a few nuggets of data I uploaded without believing they would have as large of a consequence as they did. 

[b]Short.[/b] There’s only a little over forty minutes of game play per episode, and with five episodes, this leads to roughly four hours of gameplay (assuming you don’t replay events). I follow a rule of thumb of at least $1 to 1 hour of gameplay, so in that regard, it’s a bit pricey. Just wait for a sale. 

[h1]Remark:[/h1] [b]Play in one sitting[/b] (or as close to that as possible, if you don't have a full 4-5 hours to dedicate to one game) The flow and length of the game lends itself to be optimally played in one sitting. Taking a break and not have a comprehensive refresher (like the cinematic playbacks of key choices in [i]Telltale[/i] games) of your choices and actions is jarring to the enjoyment of the storyline in my opinion.

[h1]Conclusion:[/h1]
[b]I’d recommend buying [i]Orwell[/i] when on sale.[/b] It has an interesting and captivating storyline, despite some need of polishing. The interface, flow, and artwork lend itself to be an immersive experience into the lives of the people you are spying on to protect. Also, the current social commentary gives a real-world depth to the game. It does feel a bit restricting at times, and the story is short. The save system leaves much to be desired, since I would like to more easily explore all possibilities of my choices. But, despite these factors it was still enjoyable and fun to play.
