game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I've always been one to read all of the books/letters/e-mails in games, but they rarely do more than build the world or give character backstory. I also tend to agonize over decisions in dialogue trees, worried that the "wrong" answer will cut me off from more interesting story lines. Orwell is a game that completely commits to reading and interpreting as the primary game mechanics. It succeeds at telling a satisfying story, even if it sometimes trips on the complexities of these mechanics as storytelling tools.

There are issues: The interface isn't as robust as you would hope. For instance, you can drag pictures of people from the Web into their profile, but only certain ones. At one point I found pictures of two new "persons of interest" on their corporation's website, but I couldn't drag their photos into their profiles. The game also runs into the issue that we have expectations of what can be done on the Internet. For instance, when you get the ability to break into someone's phone and can see where they've been, you expect that the addresses will tell you what is actually at those locations, but Orwell doesn't tell you this, you have to either remember or infer what is there.  

You can also get trapped when the story tries to funnel you to a certain plot point. In one part of the game there was nothing for me to do but to choose between two pieces of conflicting information: Which of two people organized a protest? The problem is that there was no way for me to make that call, it was pure he said/she said. I had a hunch, but it wasn't backed by any concrete information, and given what I had come to realize was the black-and-white nature of the Orwell system, I wanted to have something concrete before making this decision. Unfortunately, in order to progress the story I was forced to make the call based on nothing more than a hunch. 

And sometimes it seems like you need to make the wrong choice when one set of conflicting information would clearly open up a whole new tangent and the conflicting data wouldn't, so you choose the first even though you know the second is just as likely to be correct. For instance, at one point a character was accused of being gay, but there was conflicting information that he actually had a wife and kids. Of course, these two things don't conflict at all, there are plenty of gay people who have been in heterosexual relationships and even marriages. In fact, this character left his wife and children and the accusation that he was gay came many years later, so clearly one could argue that he left his wife and family BECAUSE he was gay. But in order to progress the story and open up profiles on the wife and learn more about that part of his life, I had to choose the wife data over the gay data. 

Sometimes the AI just breaks, especially that of your handler, Symes. For instance, one time I added the info that a certain character had a new girlfriend, that he wasn't with his old girlfriend, Juliet. Symes chimed in that he never knew that this character and Juliet were a couple, but I had put that information in both of their profiles a long time ago. And sometimes Symes is just clueless: At one point we discovered the name of a new character, one for whom we previously only knew her online handles, and he said something like "So she's been hiding her real name, eh?" Of course she was! Who always uses their real name for their online accounts?

It seems that there are probably multiple endings, but I only played it through once. There are no manual saves, so to get other endings you would have to play through the whole game again, which I'm not interested in doing. I wasn't entirely satisfied with my ending, but I still think that the journey was compelling and timely, probably more timely than the developers even realized when they started working on it. Orwell is a fascinating experience, especially if you are at all interested in our current information culture and the balance between government data gathering and personal privacy.

The only thing I have found nice in this game is the interface. Aside from that, there is little meat around the bone.

I've seen free games on Kongregate that are longer to finish than this game. Also, it's another of these incompleted games that comes into chapters... I mean come on! This ain't a graphic-based game, surely you can publish a complete game... it's just text damnit! I know games in the 1980s that were deeper than this!

Where is the gaming industry heading anyways with such tiny games? Make this thing free. If I can get bigger better games for free, why should I pay for this?

It seems linear, at least I did not see any changes... reminds me of The Walking Dead series minus the interactions.

I cannot recommend this "game" until it is finished and takes as much time as it costs in dollars in hours. I,ve asked for a refund. My thematic boardgame prototype has more text, depth and replayability than this computer game, I am not even paid to do it.

Don't buy until the full game is here otherwise you will be disappointed with this 30 min game... go play free games on Kongregate instead, much more fun and cheaper.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
I bought the game on sale for 8€ and finished the story within 4hrs.

Pros:

+Important and contemporary message in the light of NSA scandals and the demise of privacy in general.
+Choice matters
+Original gameplay offers a new take on the genre of text adventures.
+Nice interface
+Unique design


Cons:

-The hacking and surveilance parts are way off. In a game like this I would've hoped for more realism.
-Even though choice matters you're being guided by your supervisor in the game. You can withhold information from him but whenever I felt like doing that it was a piece of information mandatory for the story to continue. At 2-way story-forks the most interesting option often was missing I felt, which again lead to the feeling of being railroaded.
-Almost every bit of information you put into the system is commented by a pop-up comment of your supervisor which becomes a nuisance rather quickly.


Conclusion:

I really wanted to like this game. The theme of George Orwells "1984" is more relevant than ever. However I feel like the games tries too hard to hammer home their point of everybody being "frameable" by using one unforseeable plot-twist after another, which again is due to the supervisor railroading you. Also I would rather pay like 5€ more and have the tapped phone calls be actual phone calls instead of reading through live transcipts.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This one's a "buy it only on sale" for me. I would pick a neutral option were it available.

It's important to understand that Orwell is not a puzzle game inasmuch as a visual novel, and from what I understand of Steam's userbase (or at least its most vocal negative reviews), this will come as a disappointment to some people. There is very little analysis involved; you are told what and whom to investigate and any conclusions about what you discover are more or less made for you. Orwell: Keeping an Eye on You also fairly short for a $10 title, with very little replayability. Halfway through the game I still thought I was in the tutorial until I glanced at the list of achievements which indicated otherwise.

In Orwell, you are tasked with finding the culprit of a recent bombing using a top secret surveillance system also called ORWELL. Specifically, you must build profiles of potential suspects based on their social media profiles, online accounts, and personal devices. This is done by selecting relevant excerpts, called datachunks, and "uploading" them to the ORWELL server. Meanwhile, your "advisor," a man called Symes, will review what you send and make important decisions based on this info. What information you choose to upload and when you upload it will affect the lives of the people you investigate and the dangerous events unfolding in "real time."

Unfortunately, your advisor is an idiot. I mean, he seems nice enough, but he's incredibly trigger-happy, and views the act of merely uploading information to compile a detailed suspect profile as an indictment in itself. "Woah, she changed her hair color? Good info, I've just sent out the warrant for her arrest."

Because of this and other aspects of gameplay where the importance of particular actions is not especially well telegraphed, most of my game-changing decisions were followed by an "oh crap, I did not just mean to do that. I hope I can fix it later!"

When control over a sandbox environment and its inhabitants is so apparently arbitrary, your first playthrough is no longer a personal journey and a reflection of your choices. Instead it is a hilarious spectacle of disastrous butterfly effects outpacing your sad and frantic attempts at damage control. This is great in a series like Hitman, though not so much in a game trying to make a point about the deadly shortsightedness of relying on a digital panopticon.

Orwell's conceit is ultimately that even a government allowed to so thoroughly investigate its private citizens may still fail to meet the outcomes that were supposed to justify the dissolution of privacy. The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good.

The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that:

ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer.

You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision.

As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed.

Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility.

On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise.

By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

The truth can still elude even the most advanced surveillance systems, as it does here, and so any drastic actions carried out in the name of safety may do more harm than good. The problem is that it tries to demonstrate this through a system made deliberately inept in the service of its plot and political message. EDIT: So I'm an idiot and apparently you can arrest the true mastermind in Episode 5 provided you have enough luck and/or second playthrough foresight. However, it's not especially intuitive (the 20 datachunk limit doesn't help!), and requires some deviation from the stated goal in a game which has been so far entirely based on completing the stated goal in some form or another and which otherwise restricts your ability to freely investigate, in that: ORWELL will only allow access to new resources once you have added a related datachunk, and even then this selection is limited by what the clumsy "AI" (read: the story) deems relevant. The AI also determines which pieces of information are selectable for use as datachunks. The result is like a crime-solving version of Chopped, wherein you must come up with your best answer given a random handful of documents. You are only able to pursue a line of thinking that the AI believes is relevant, and the AI has been written to provide the wrong answer. You can't get much out of the stuff you're forced to work with, either, as advisors will only let you investigate people they deem worthy at the time (rest assured you will still get the blame every time something bad happens!), and with each datachunk you index in the hopes of unlocking new documents or comments, you run the risk of your advisor making an unpredictably dangerous and irreversible decision. As a result, Orwell depicts not so much the shortcomings of overly-invasive surveillance tech as it does the flaws in this particular system which has been deliberately badly designed. Usually writers in the "techno-voyeurism genre" can look forward to populating a lot of fake apps and web pages with filler data which serves no plot purpose except to flesh out the in-game universe and hide easter eggs. So I understand the choice for the developers to omit that open browsing capability from a practical point of view -- but it does come at a cost to Orwell's credibility. On the positive side, Orwell has a cute low-poly aesthetic and its UI is both visually appealing and well organized, especially given what a tremendous challenge it must have been to elegantly display so much information. The soundtrack works well and effectively manages to convey dramatic tone shifts (usually from "lalala browsing someone's timeline" to "oh NO A BOMB IS ABOUT TO GO OFF IN THIRTY SECONDS!!"). I also like that there are achievements of equal calibre for most major story outcomes, "good" or otherwise. By all means get Orwell if you enjoy techno-voyeurism (does this genre have an actual name?); you might find it to be a fun time-waster. I might pick up season 2... on sale... eventually. I just don't think it would appeal to general audiences at its current price point, or that it's particularly effective in delivering its themes.

review_text_raw:
Long story short: Great interactive [b]novel[/b]. Very addicting and compelling storytelling.

Long story ahead:
But, is this a game? And if it is a game what is the [i]enjoyment[/i] a player could have from playing it?

I have three main references as game definition:
[list]
[*][quote]Games are an exercise of voluntary control systems, in which there is a contest between powers, confined by rules in order to produce a disequilibrial outcome.
—Elliot Avedon and Brian Sutton-Smith[/quote]
[*][quote]A game is an interactive structure of endogenous meaning that requires players to struggle toward a goal.
—Greg Costikyan[/quote]
[*][quote]
A game is a closed, formal system, that engages players in structured conflict, and resolves in an unequal outcome.
—Tracy Fullerton, Chris Swain, and Steven Hoffman[/quote]
[/list]
Maybe you are questioning yourself why should I to struggle to classify Orwell as a game or as an interactive novel. The reply is really simple: because it changes a lot the review. And just because Orwell is very borderline I will review it twice, one review as an interactive novel and one as a game letting the reader to choose what fits best.

[b]Orwell as an interactive graphic novel[/b]
The story is really interesting and compelling, keeping you addicted to it until the end.

The novel is [i]pretty short[/i], I have walkthrough it twice in less than 11 hours, but when the storytelling is strong, able to immerse the reader, shortness is not an issue.

The music is nice, but a bit [i]repetitive[/i], above all when you hear mostly the same loop for hours, broken for short time by a drama loop.

Maybe this interactive novel is a bit too much expensive, but it is strongly suggested if you are able to get it on sale.


[b]Orwell as a game[/b]
Pros:
[list]
[*]Story
[/list]
Cons:
[list]
[*]Lack of choice and freedom
[*]Event based system and strong linear game, if you don't do what is expected the story does not go on
[*]Less than 8 hours of gameplay to get to the end (first time you play, otherwise a lot less)
[*]Max of 3-4 replays before having seen all what the game has to offer meaning less than 20/25 hours of total gameplay.
[*]Music: 1 main repetitive theme loop + some other drama stings...
[/list]

I am sorry but being this sold as a game I couldn't [b]honestly[/b] suggest to buy it, and anyway as I have already written as an interactive novel is a bit too much expensive.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw: Before buying this game, I saw that most of the top rated reviews just spoke about comparison's to Orwellian works, modern social networks, and Papers Please. And I thought important to address a couple of things after playing through what is available. Orwell is an episodic game; meaning, this is not the final result. This is more of a "Whodunit" than a Thriller mystery, so judging it for linearity might be unfair since they attempt to make you the detective by providing you with a given set of aesthetics. Now talking about aesthetics, this game/experience has its obvious references to Orwell and "1984" -- mainly -- but it is very clear they are only used for inspiration. This is no de facto Orwell Fan Fiction, just an experienced based on some questions the devs had about resembling aspects of society. From the two episodes they have released, I can tell that this is comparable to Papers Please in that you have to provide an analysis to come up with game altering decisions. However, since this is a "Whodunit" type mystery, and are limited to less than half of the intended story arc, we cannot truly make that comparison. What I can say without spoiling, is that there are choices that can either save or spare hundreds of lives, and the deciding factor is actually a juxtaposition of logic I have yet to fully grasp and understand. I think this is a great game; yet, it remains an aesthetic experience we are not yet able to finalise. I look forward for Episode 3's release in three day's time.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1] Prelude:	[/h1]
For too long Telltale have had a vice grip on linear story-based games. Which is a shame considering only about 2 of their games were decent. So when I heard a new game had created enough favorable reviews and praise from people I trust, I decided to boot up: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You, or rather, Orwell: generic subtitle. 

[h1] Gameplay:	[/h1]
The game consists of reading through text, selecting infomation to upload to Orwell, a huge data base supposedly allowing to keep endless amounts of infomation on people (more on this later) you select outlined text or images, and choose wether or not to upload the data. Most of the infomation is required, but the game does a fairly decent job of shaking things up, infomation conflicting and choosing which one is most significant, the worst choice being: An online commenter calls guy A 'homosexual' meanwhile in a newspaper, it is stated he has been happily married with children. You choose which source is reliable. There also ends up being a data mechanic, only alloweed to upload 20 data chunks. The game does a [u] really [/u] good job of rewarding the player to go further, for instance near the end of the second chapter ([b] SPOILERS [/b]): [spoiler] There is a bomb detonating soon, with two people potentially offering locations of the bomb, if you dig deep into the email or messages (I think) of the people, you can see him admitting that he let his idea be pushed down, then using dates and timestamps, you can figure out this was just after the two people offered the locations. 	[/spoiler] This not only makes the player feel great after solving this puzzle, but also affects the endgame too. However the endgame is EASILY the weakest part of the game.

It is the [u] exact [/u] game issue as telltale games, maybe even worse. On the nose the character's tell you what you did, so averty it feels stupid. Not to mention.. [spoiler] The secret ending is locked off depending on how you handled a situation in Chapter 3, where you have to actively fail at your job to reach the good ending telling the police that a woman is armed and has knowledge of military which is FACT, you have to actively NOT tell the police this info, and THEN tell them her correct location, despite the fact the character says: 'I am not going down without a fight.' And you can accidentally trigger endings randomly, with supposedly 3/4 choices layed down right at the end, then wanting to do extra research, it doesn't say 'Are you sure, this will end?' Or something like that.	[/spoiler]

[h1] Graphics:	[/h1]
These devs are smart, at least in this department. The game is extremely stylised, meaning it will age very well. There was one time where I wasn't sure who was in a picture due to this, and it came as a suprise to me. Otherwise a few issues, there is no voice acting, even on phone calls. This shouldn't be an issue, considering other MAJOR review sites can get away with subtracting points from a game for having good voice acting rather than nothing. (yeah im still angry) If you also have Dyslexia maybe give this one a miss, it is a LOT of reading, and if you dislike the font, it doesn't change often enough to merit trying with this one.

[h1] Other:	[/h1]
The soundtrack starts off great, being the perfect sort of tracks for reading, not distracting enough to take you out of the game, but enough to stand on it's own. There is a few 'sting tracks' where they are used for shock, and this works mostly, apart from near the end where you are simply scrolling down and then you see some text and DUNNN, which was suprising and took the shock out of what I was reading because I didn't have to read it in time. It also starts getting REALLY repetitive near the end.

The game REALLY tries to be replayable, with the ability to skip to chapters 1-5, but a big problem are the phone calls, they average around 4.5 minuites in real time. With the final one, Chapter 5, where you would WANT to go through again first, too see if it could have ended different lasts around 10 minuites, of non-interactable text, which you would have read already. The game also isn't too long, if you read every article and looked indepth for everything I can imagine it lasting at around 5 hours, if you skip text and just look at the highlighted text, around 3 hours. For me, my playthrough was around 4.7 hours. A decent time, not too long, not too short.

[h1] TL:DR:	[/h1]
If you enjoy linear story-based games and want to see a good attempt or just a LINEAR STORY GAME WITHOUT TELLTALE IN IT, and enjoy reading, then its a recommendation, if you don't fit all 3 of those criteria, wait until a Steam Sale, or a Humble Bundle like I did. It does hint at some cool political ideas and ideologies, but that's more in the sequal.

Nevertheless, I look forward for the next Orwell game to go on sale and be fully out, I am a cautious fan, please keep up the good work devs, nice to see some varation in the gaming scene. You seem like cool guys too, patching stuff in and so forth.

-Thanks for reading
-Cain

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
This game really does sell the vibe that you're an analyst working inside of Orwell's system, while never feeling tedious or contrived, a big achievement in my book. But of course, the real pull of a game like this is its ability to explore difficult themes about freedom of expression, security, surveillance, checks and balances, etc...

I found the narrative compelling and nuanced. The gameplay effectively branches narratives based on the prejudices of the player and it was interesting to see how an individual with different philosophies might simply follow a different rabbit hole, never stumbling upon the same "truths" that I had. In presenting the narrative this way, the creators wrote a fair bit of nuance into the story: little arcs that can be easily missed if someone's inclined one way or another on a controversial subject. The tension between the themes is reasonably well managed and the endings express different morals; I find the decision to not conclusively state a moral position to be quite brave from the creators' parts and such a decision serves the broader concept of the game very well. 

In considering games as art, I think Orwell provides an excellent example of an expression that is best explored through the medium of video games. Orwell feels like a fledgling OS, simple, sleek, intuitive as an Apple product, creepy and intrusive as a Google one. As a user, you are complicit in the structures of surveillance and, while you have some authority on how to navigate the complex moral questions in front of you (and in doing so, revealing your own biases), there is a palpable sense that this apparatus is large, amorphous, and exuding a sense of clinical evil that only exists with oppressive regimes or corporations. In other words, this game conveys appropriately both the individual and systemic realities of mass surveillance. Now onto my main gripe.

The characters are all viciously annoying human beings. While I certainly understand that in order to create a game with significant nuance in the face of large, controversial themes, individual characters almost necessarily have to retain both positive and negative qualities (a very human characterization), I nevertheless ended up finding the characters insufferable. If my ID had its way, these asshats would all be jailed simply for being pompous, room-temperature IQ, morons with the total and absolute inability to make a single correct decision in their lives. Even characters I initially found likeable or at least, found myself agreeing with, ended up talking their way into these childish and absurd holes and given that the characters are crucial to the gameplay and their interactions are the basis for plot advancement, I often found reading their texts quite a drag. 

Overall, a solid exploration of difficult themes through a very effective medium. Props to the creators for their creativity, narrative complexity, and willingness to engage with controversial subjects without tribalism or devolving into virtue-signaling. I especially like how the game exposes your own biases (though never in an explicit manner). May Hancock slowly rot into agonizing, ego-shattering insanity as he's thrown into the darkest dungeon.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Intresting premise,  poor execution. In the attempt to create stakes for the players decision, Orwell goes out of it's way to obfuscate or even fail to present clarfying information until after the decision is made. It also prevents refinement of past data with new context. Being forced to compete in the 20 meter jump to conclusions in order to find the context you needed to make that conclusion is beyond obxnoxious. This is made worse by there being minimal clarity to what the data you've supplied will be intreperted as, and that intreptation is final with little abitliy to recontextualize. 

This of course undermines any moral arguement the game attempts to present or have you consider. Over surveillance, the effect of technology on the governments ability to monitor it's citizens and so forth are good topics to explore. However demonstarting the conquences by forcing the player to pick up the idiot ball does no one any favours.  

The concept is good, if you can deal with being forced to make uncontextualized leaps of judgement you might enjoy the game. But the inability to use good inquirial practices like preserving and rexamining conflicting data in light of new evidence kills the game for me.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
What a wasted opportunity.

I went into this game wanting to like it - I really did. To be clear - I played through the entire game, finishing each of the 5 chapters.

Orwell is ostensibly a game about a surveillance state gone terribly wrong - but almost at every opportunity, it fails to make any meaningful point and constantly gets in its own way.

It starts bad. Rather than giving you, as a player, the agency to incriminate and potentially ruin the lives of the people you are surveilling, the game immediately puts you at arms-length. You are nothing more than a data collector with the ability to find and store information, but not make any meaningful analysis or conclusions about this data. Worse, it pairs you with the clumsily-written and drearily heavy-handed Symes - the *actual* investigator, who acts on the information you upload and is a constant source of awkward, immersion-breaking, and stupid commentary. 

It's true that, in principle, the data you choose to upload can affect the lives and outcomes of the people whose privacy you're invading - the trouble is that there's no real incentive to do so. Oftentimes, you must upload certain pieces of data in order to move the story along - which makes sense, because you're nothing more than a glorified data monkey clicking blue text and throwing it into a database. If you choose to hide a piece of information, it's not clear whether or not you'll be able to progress through the story. If you get something wrong (in the extremely limited range of things you are even allowed to get wrong), there are few consequences - an issue exacerbated by how distanced you are from everything that goes down. You don't really get to make the call, figure out the deduction, or even choose whether or not you should be wielding the awesome power you do. You either progress the story, or you don't - Symes is the one who gets to actually decide.

What's worse is that each of the characters in the game are utterly unlikable - the crimes you investigate them for are legitimate crimes that hurt real innocents and pose genuine dangers to the society in which they inhabit - the moral quandary that this game should so naturally lend itself to (the invasion of privacy, the loss of intimacy, that everybody is a criminal under mass surveillance, etc.,) is utterly and absolutely wasted. Instead, you are railroaded through a specific set of documents, webpages, and chats (not giving you any opportunity to actually deduce anything) in which not one of the horribly written characters manages to endear themselves.

Ultimately, this game is trying to tell you two stories - a by the numbers B-grade mystery plot filled with unlikable and annoying characters, and a study of the evolution of mass surveillance in an increasingly tech-focussed society. In so doing, they tell neither one well. They did an incredible disservice to a barely-interesting character study of modern revolutionaries, and an even greater disservice to the core (and seemingly obvious!) issues with state-driven, indiscriminate surveillance.

Let's not even start with the UI. What begins as a somewhat interesting ability to listen in on conversations quickly becomes a tiresome and arduous chore - there are a couple of moments in which listening in on a conversation live makes sense, but these moments are few and far between. For the most part, you are treated to a disastrously slow chat message filled with stilted dialogue and unfortunate Fellow Kids idioms, or an equally slow voice transcription. I quickly began to dread these moments, rather than feel the rush of uncovering a potential clue.

At no point do you feel like a data wizard, an unscrupulous detective, or even a curious and detached researcher. You just feel bored. 

Orwell is, despite its polished presentation, a total and undeniable bust. 

Desperately trying to cram all of the social commentary it should have been exploring over the entire game into its final chapter, it fails to make a meaningful statement about mass surveillance and the police state. 

Having written shallow, stupid, stereotypical characters with zero likable traits or humanizing aspects (each of whom are also genuine suspects in an act of actual terrorism) it fails to present a compelling character study of the 21st-century revolutionary.

By railroading you during every part of the core gameplay loop and anchoring you at the waist with a bumbling, intrusive character (who gets to make *all* the calls and draw all the *actual* conclusions), they fail to provide a satisfying, thrilling, or even baseline interesting detective experience.

Finally, by forgetting the most fundamental principles in their clunky, limited, and careless design, they failed to provide an even halfway tolerable interface. 

I didn't even get to enjoy interacting with the game.

Orwell is a disaster. You will get nothing from it, no insight, no emotion, no deductions, and no surprises. It wastes every bit of the opportunity it had to say something meaningful.

This is my Two Minutes Hate - and Orwell deserves every second of it.

review_text_raw:
A good game in principle but fell short along the way.

I really wanted to like this game more.
Initially I was very intrigued, however the longer I played the more everything started to fall apart.
First off - this needs voice acting.
I don't think every line in the game needs voice acting, but at least the phone calls and the advisers should've been voiced.
Secondly - add more red herrings/alternative plot lines that a player can trip on.
This game initially seemed very vast and branched out to me, yet as I played it through and then replayed a couple more times for the achievements I realised that it is still very linear and there's not much you can do that will have a very big effect on your playthrough.
Third - there were a few plot lines in the game that were just never explained or touched on again. I think the game could've been more fleshed out if these plotlines were explored more.
Fourth - not being able to change datachunks. I understand that the whole plot is built on the idea that you cannot keep changing data, but it just felt like an artificial boundary for seemingly no reason.
Lastly - I couldn't help but feel like some of the writing for the characters was just off (it's hard to put into words but something just didn't feel right about the way the interactions went).

Overall the game was ok, but its just not something I would recommend to someone else.

review_text_raw:
I've been wanting to write a short but to the point review for this game. Mostly because I rarely finish any games in one go. 

Orwell is [b]NOT[/b] going to WOW you. It's not mindblowing, mind you. It will, however, keep you intrigued once you decide to give it a try. 

[u]What's it about?[/u]

It's heavily influenced by the reveals of Edward Snowden. It's about working in the NSA and uncovering personal data in order to get to the truth. It's about whether or not as people we'd sacrifice our "freedom" or our "safety". Overall, an interesting premise.

[u]Right. It's a game, so what's the gameplay like?[/u]

The "game" consists of reading a lot of text and putting certain bits of it together in order to progress to the next chapters. It doesn't sound too engaging but once you start reading through it, it is able to drag you into its universe. There are multiple endings and choices where you need to choose what to reveal for the people you gather information yourself. 

[u]Multiple choices. Does that mean there's a lot of replayability?[/u]

Well, once you get to the conclusion, you sort of feel fulfilled, hence why many of the reviewers of this game have a few hours of gametime. [b]BUT[/b] I think you can easily play the game a second time to do a few things differently. There is some replayability potential.

Good soundtrack, interesting premise, amusing characters, nice artstyle, engaging storyline. I strongly recommend this game if you want something different.

review_text_raw:
[b]Guys!  Perhaps this may come as a shock to some of you but, in case you didn’t know, this game has a bit of an agenda….[/b] 
Ok ok, joking aside I bought Orwell a while back when it fell below my “if I buy this and don’t like it, I won’t feel any great loss” threshold.  It sat in my library untouched until a rainy day when I didn’t feel like getting into anything too involved.  I say this to admit that I went into this with pretty bland expectations.  

I generally view games like this the way I do a book from an unknown author, but that has a premise I like.  I knew going in that the game makers had a point to make and even though it was a point I generally agree with, I was a little wary.  [i]I don’t like being preached at, so I wasn’t sure if I was going to spend the entire game being beat over the head with the rhetoric bat whilst being presented with billboards saying in big bold letters “Hey look, the authors feel very strongly about this” at every turn or if the game would have any merit beyond the political statement.[/i]  [b]I’m very thankful to say that this game was far more than just a tray upon which to serve political and social commentary and it was even very clever in doing so.[/b]

So why did I start out with all that waffle about political commentary?  Because I want to set the tone for how I approached the game and the preconceptions I had going in.  I went into the experience thinking that I pretty much had them figured out and that I would easily be able to see through any “hard choices with lasting consequences” to what the authors were really trying to sell to the player.  And chapter 1 pretty much was just that.  I “knew” they were trying to get me to suspect a particular person and that they wanted me to assume the simple answer so they could jump out from behind the posterized, low-polygon trees and say “Ha!  See how even with all the information at your fingertips you jumped to the wrong conclusion.”  So naturally I did just the opposite.  Purposefully ignoring what I assumed were red-herrings and by the end of chapter 1, I’d almost lost interest figuring that I had it all figured out.  I was delighted, and a bit disappointed, that I was wrong.  

Starting chapter 2, I was actually engaged in the narrative and was now determined not to be caught off-guard again.  I still knew there was a point to it all, but I wasn’t as sure I knew what that point was.  By the end of the game, I knew what was going on, but because I’d fed information to orwell earlier on that seemed harmless at the time, I’d built a profile on some of the characters that was not incorrect but was misrepresentative.  This led to events playing out in a way that I didn’t want and with no way to go back and correct.  I felt duped, but in a good way.  The game had indeed gotten it’s point across, but in a very subtle and engaging way that left me still feeling that I enjoyed the experience.

So let’s sum this up, shall we? 
•	Orwell was well worth the money
•	Gameplay was not nearly as on-rails as I had expected
•	Story was actually very engaging and believable
•	Plot twists did not feel super-contrived simply to force the player to be wrong for the sake of proving a point.  All the plot twists could have been seen coming I think if the user had paid attention to the details and not just focused on what Orwell highlights.
•	The game actually made me think and didn’t preach it’s point smugly from contrived moral high-ground and I appreciated that.  

Here is where I would usually list a few things that could have been improved, but the game is pretty simple and the UI layout is simple and easy to use.  Some of the “websites” that you visit have clickable links that aren’t obvious… that was kind of annoying, but not too bad.  I’d like to say that I wish you could go back and edit information when you found out it was wrong, but I think it’s integral to the game the concept that YOU are the filter.  If it’s not relevant, accurate, or then you don’t upload it.  If I had one complaint it would be that I sometimes didn’t know what would “trigger” the next event and so sometimes I’d upload something I didn’t really want to just because I thought I had to in order to progress the game.   

All in all, the game took me about 6 hours to play through… you could go longer or shorter, but in the end, it’s not a great investment timewise…. In fact, it practically gives you a good stopping point between chapters.  I highly recommend the game.  It’s worth $7-10 for your time and as a good conversation starter.  Gift it to a friend so you can have a good conversation on the topic.  

Anyway, That’s my 2 cents worth.

-John

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]A great and very frightening concept
[*]Awesome story
[*]Great replayabililty
[*]The design is just beautiful
[/list]


[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
[*]First chapters get a bit stale after one or two playthroughs
[*]No way to speed up dialogue you’ve already read and just need to grab info from
[/list]

[h1]Review:[/h1]
The most terrifying part of Orwell is just how easily its events could come to pass in our own world. George Orwell himself could not have predicted the level of surveillance we all voluntarily subject ourselves to by keeping always-listening, always-tracking smart devices on our persons, in our cars, and in our homes. It doesn’t take a lot of imagination to see a system such as the one portrayed in the game being used by a real nation, especially since we know the United States already conducts mass surveillance in a multitude of ways.


Orwell (the game) did an excellent job keeping me on the edge of my seat throughout its entire duration. Even though you only interact with them (or rather, their information) through a screen, it was hard not to feel connected to the characters. Whether that connection is based on sympathy or a desire to lock them up is up to you.


The game lends itself well to multiple playthroughs in order to achieve different endings, and there are tons of different ways to get to those endings. However, by the second or third time the first few chapters begin to feel very repetitive. I often found myself checking my phone while waiting for in-game conversations to finish so I could decide which chunks of data to grab. There is tons of interesting stuff to read in Orwell, but it would be nice to skip past some dialogue when I’ve already read it three times.


The length of the game really surprised me. For $11 I didn’t expect as much story and detail as I got. While it only took me about 6 hours my first time through, and I can definitely go through quicker now if I wanted, looking over all of the great little details that have been thrown in definitely takes time. That’s not a bad thing, as Orwell’s realism is only helped by how believable its characters (and their social media profiles, emails, and phone calls) are.


This is definitely a great game, and it was an awesome surprise when I discovered it while browsing the web one day. Be warned, though - after you play you’ll often find yourself thinking about your online conversations, and if something you said years ago (or even yesterday) could somehow be used to incriminate you.

Meh.

Positively meh.  I'll be honest, I played the game for a little while and then went and read a bunch of reviews about it, and I realized that this game definitely is not for me.  At the end of the day, the concept reeled me in, but the game failed to deliver nearly as much as I thought it would.  Things are a little bit too straight forward, and there is not nearly enough depth.  Also, for as much as the game pretends that you can choose some information and ignore others, it simply isn't true.  In the early game especially, you can hit a dead end if you choose to ignore certain information, and the game does not give you any indication that there is nothing more you can do.  I wish the game would tell you when you HAD TO DO something in order to proceed.  And then, in that vein, it feels like you are playing a rail-shooter, replaced with just clicking-and-dragging information.

Worth checking out if you can get it for free or less than a dollar, but otherwise, there are probably better games you can pass your time with.  Your mileage may vary.

review_text_raw:
Here's what happens: You get told to look up this woman who may have commited a crime. You don't actually look up anything, you just click on the page it gives you. game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
ORWELL - 3/10

Quick Review:  A slightly more interactive version of a visual novel, Orwell tries to claim some of the success legendary books like 1984 and Brave New World have. Unfortunately it's cliche and boring characters, simple and tedious gameplay, long wait times and confusing target audience make this a game I can't possibly recommend.

Story
-------
You play as an investigator who is hired from outside a country where a new system called "Orwell" is put in place. In it's early stages, Orwell is being used to collect data and spy on people in order to keep the public safe. After a bomb goes off in Freedom Plaza, your job is to find who is behind the bombing by investigating someone who has a small criminal history that was at the scene and see what you can discover from there.

The story isn't particularly interesting and while there are some major plot events I don't think they hit their intended mark for me because I wasn't particularly captivated in the first place. The characters you have to investigate are all the typical "fuck the government" protesters with little to no original personality traits. Everything is unoriginal and cliche as can be.

Gameplay
--------------
Orwell is split into 5 episodes, each taking roughly around 40 minutes to an hour. You sit in front of a virtual computer screen representing the UI for Orwell, and you have to drag and drop highlighted bits of information from various pages (news articles/blogs/websites etc) in order to learn more about the people you're investigating. Some of these bits will be conflicting (highlighted in yellow, like addresses or opinions). You will have to listen in on conversations, read personal emails. You're basically just spying on people and using their profiles to learn more about them.

The gameplay is literally just drag and drop information onto the character it is relevant too. You don't even actually need to read anything because all the important information will be highlighted anyway. Conflicting information is important because it defines what happens to each character at the end of an episode but it's always easy to figure out which is right once you discover what both conflicting elements are (which the game will tell you anyway once you find both). You'll also have to listen to long, unskippable and un-fastforwadable phone calls for a tiny bit of information.

Design
---------
I think the game interface, while basic does look nice. It's entirely pale blue and means that the game doesn't feel aggressive or heavy. The soundtrack is forgettable, I turned it down pretty early to help me concentrate. The writing is actually pretty good but the characters and story is just unoriginal.

Problems
-------------
The biggest problem is that it's just boring. There barely is anything that constitutes real gameplay as all you're doing is dragging + dropping or waiting around for phone calls to end. As the story isn't very interesting (to me anyway) the further I got into the game the more of a chore it became. As I also said, almost everything is a straight appropriation of the older Orwellian style novels. I mean the game is called "Orwell". I seriously also hated having to wait around and listen to phone calls. It would've been better for the characters to have the call offscreen and you just get uploaded the transcript once you collect enough information (so phone calls would act like checkpoints; like the rest of the articles in the game do).

Achievements
-------------------
As the gameplay is almost non-existant, all achievements are based on what you decide to upload to Orwell. In the first episode if you upload all the peaceful things related to the first target you'll get an achievement, but if you upload how she suffers from PTSD or hates the government you'll get another. You will have to play each episode at least twice (the third episode needs to be played 3 times). Luckily there is chapter select so no achievement is missable, and the achievements are all self-contained in each chapter so choices made in chapter 1 have no impact on achievements for later chapters. I think the achievement list is pretty good.

Summary
-------------
I don't know who this game is targeted towards. If you like reading, then you've probably read 1984 OR Brave New World and as this game is basically an updated version of the book there's no need to play it. If you don't like reading then you won't like this game. I like reading, I have the BIGGEST and STRONGEST brain and i've read alot of intellectual stimuli and I still couldn't get into this game. It just does NOTHING that isn't seen in 1984 or BNW. I guess if those books are literally the best books you've ever read then you might like this but if not i'd stay away.

review_text_raw:
One of the game’s themes is how people present themselves online as well as offline. This is no more evident than with the various interactions the small groups of characters have with each other in the game. Cassandra Watergate is, on one hand, an emotionally unstable, childish woman who does not care about adult responsibility, but on the other hand she is an activist who might have been responsible for a series of bombings and assaults on police.

Which character is the real one? That is what makes the story interesting. Orwell sets up characters that behave in unique ways, behaviour patterns that often conflict with your perception and then ask you to decide who they are. People are different online and in the presence of other people. Orwell uses limited perception and distorted character presentation to make the player want to continue playing.

The gameplay itself is quite easy and straight-forward. You use Orwell to find data on various people supposedly involved in terrorist activities, in order to uncover who's responsible and who's not. Relevant information is highlighted in blue. Orwell might be easy, but that does not make it any less interesting. Simple, but very polished.

The game has an idea, but it gets repetitive quite fast. A 5/10.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
[h1]Preface[/h1]
This review is being written before the conclusion of the game in episode five. I've played through the first four episodes a couple times exploring different outcomes, however, as episode five is not out yet I'm not able to comment on the totallity of the story.

[h1]The Machine[/h1]
[b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] has a very close [url=http://www.cbs.com/shows/person_of_interest/]Person of Interest[/url] vibe. The government of the fictitious country has obtained a Machine, or System, that surveils the populous gathering information however it does not act on the gathered information. The idea of the game is that the system, aptly named [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b], isn't able to decern human subtlety, sarcasim, or deciet. As such, the fictious government has [b]outsourced[/b] the task of resolving conflicts in the data, and identifying what is relevant and what is not. You as the player take on this role as an outsider to the country, tasked with sifting through the data that [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] gives you access to inorder to identify person(s) of interest. This is a role somewhat like [i]Person of Interest[/i]'s Harold Finch.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is Not[/h1]
I've seen several complaints that the game isn't challenging enough, many comparing it to several "hacker simulators" such as [b][i]Hacknet[/i][/b] or [b][i]UPLINK[/i][/b]. On the surface the concept might seem somewhat similar to games such as these, however, this is not what [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] is. In this game you are not doing any "hacking" or "cracking", that is [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b]'s job. You are more of a data analyst telling a hacker, that happens to be a computer system, what data is relevant and linked to certian people. Treating it in the same vein as other "hacker simulators" isn't fair to the game and if that is what you are expecting, you will be dissapointed.

[h1]What [i]Orwell[/i] Is[/h1]
So if [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] isn't a "hacker simulator" what is it? I've also seen the categorization as a "visual novel" which is much closer to what this game is. The game play is reminiscent of [url=https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Choose_Your_Own_Adventure]Choose Your Own Adventure[/url] books some of you might have read as a child. As such, the outcomes that occur in the game depend on what data you choose to "flag" or "link" to someone as relevant. This process will estabilsh relationships between persons of interest that may uncover new motivations, or might change the context of the data you have available. The game is about you being the guiding hand for a surveillance system tasked with preventing & solving crime.

[h1]Pros[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Interesting visual style
    [*]Enjoyable storyline that feels very linear (as it should), but leaves you with a sprinkling of "what if" moments where you feel things could have been different.
    [*]Fairly Intuitive gameplay.
[/list]

[h1]Cons[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Somewhat short, although there is some replay value if you want to try to achieve different outcomes from prior play through(s)
    [*]You aren't able to link data to someone until [b][i]Orwell[/i][/b] identifies it as potentially relevant.
    [*]You aren't able to revise or change "known" data based on new information
    [*]You aren't able to alter "data conflicts" if you find additional information
    [*]No "Save Game" system, uses the idea of profiles instead to allow for differing play throughs
[/list]

[h1]Conclusion[/h1]
The game is a fun and enjoyable experience if you do not have unrealistic expectations of what the game is and what the gameplay is like. It offers an interesting and thought provoking social commentary on the age of information technology that we live in. The game presents the idea of freedom & privacy -vs- surveillance & security in an interesting and fairly balanced way. If you actually think about what you are doing moment-by-moment in the game, you will likely find yourself re-evaluating your thoughts on these topics. That isn't to say this game is going to challenge your views or change your mind, simply that you will likely find yourself thinking about these topics and why you hold your views on these topics.

If you enjoy naritive driven experiences this game will likey fit well in your games library. While there are some things the game could certianly do better I didn't find these issues to detract significantly from the games main draw for me, it's story & premise. I would like to see the game updated with some sort of "Save Game" system that would allow you to "branch off" after each chapter within a single profile. This would make exploring different outcomes easier, howerver, I also can see that this goes against the linear nature of the games concept. The game strives to make you feel like you are participating in the events, that are time bound and as such linear in nature, which have consequences.

Overall I'm enjoying the game and would recommend it to those who enjoy adventure games, visual novels, and mysteries. This isn't really a problem/puzzle solving game (like a "hacker simulator") so if that is what you are looking for you may wish to pass on this game. I definitely recommend it for what it is and I'm really looking forward to the culmination of these events in episode five.

game_name: Orwell: Keeping an Eye On You
review_text_raw:
Orwell is a detective Interactive Fiction game, where you assume a role of a goverment-employed ivestigator with an emergancy right to access citizens' devices and Internet activity.
You are tasked with finding a person responsible for a terrorist attack in a fictional city of Bonton in a fictional Nation.
The game has a really solid mechanic for gathering and sorting information, that I have personally not seen before. Your main power is collecting bits and pieces of the info in documents, on websites, in messges and voicecall transcriptions. You need to compare and analyze different sources that are often conflicting and rarely fully truthfull, keeping in mind context, biases, possible angles. The coolest parts is that instead of acting on the info, you only relay it to your supperiors who make all the calls. So in order to achieve the outcome you want, you need to basically socially ingeneer your bosses by spoon-feeding them the info that will shape their worldview. 
I feel that it's a powerful metaphor on how the perseption influences action, and how malicious forces may take advantage of the powers to shape perseption. Especially when they can control the information for the people in position of power — through media, narratives or implicit biases. 
This is the main win of the game — it explores an important concept via its engaging detective gameplay.
I do have some criticisms, or rather some notes based on my own expectations. I first came into this game expecting it to be a mostly realistic tale with a bit of the antiutopic twist. And while it certainly presents realistic aesthetic, the deeper you go into this world and plot, the more outlandish things become. This is genre fiction through and through. Observing real totalitarian regimes as they implement digital survaillance, and seeing real opposition and its struggles in such countries... Well, simplifications and assumptions Orwell makes, they just shatter believability of the whole premise. Some things just raise questions (or eybrows) even with everyday logic, such as the game's fictional geography. It somehow includes a Central-European coated country, a Slavic Eastern-European and a (sort-of) Middle-Eastern or Central-Asian (?) countiry just neighboring each others — without the cross-influence that this fact might bring. It also includes references to real states such as Germany and South Africa. A bit of a tonal clash.
But if you accept genre conventions and treat this as a pulp fiction detective story, it really opens up as a nice and fun exploration of some important topics of current society. All while being a pretty cool Interactive Fiction game.

Pros:
- The game brings awareness to important social problems: surveillance and totalitarianism
- Music is OK
- The characters are relatable
- Story is realistic
- This implementation of mass surveillance is plausible

- Lack of depth in decision. The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value.
- Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics.
- The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. 
- Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency.
- The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible.
- The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready.

The game is basically linear, except the ending which is a binary moral choice. No replay value. - Lack of immersion stemming from weak game mechanics. - The conflict system makes no sense and works against realisticity. How in the world can the system predict that something is in conflict with an unknown data chunk? A conflict should only be shown when both data chunks are known. - Phone calls wait for you to tap, such as everything in this game. No time pressure or feeling of urgency. - The web is way too small, and computer hacking is way too minimalistic to be plausible. - The enjoyment as you progress is almost a total downward slope. I think the last episode and the ending is just not ready. - Game lasts no more than 8 hours.
